triage.name: Bacterial conjunctivitis
triage.reason: Common red eye presentation with discharge; diagnosis reachable by history, exam and, when needed, cultures, with important look-alikes such as viral and allergic conjunctivitis.

demographics: Very common in young children, especially those in daycare or school
Adults of any age can be affected, with higher rates in contact lens wearers

risk_factors.text: Close contact with someone who has conjunctivitis

exposures: Contact with a person who has red eye or eye discharge
Contaminated contact lens solutions or cases

chief_complaints.text: My eye is red and stuck shut
There is yellow-green goop coming from my eye
My eye feels scratchy and irritated

hpi.duration: Usually less than 1 week at presentation
hpi.progression: Starts in one eye with redness and discharge, then may spread to the other eye within a few days
hpi.quality: Gritty, burning, or foreign-body sensation; discharge is thick and purulent
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; vision is typically unaffected
hpi.timing: Constant, worse in the morning when discharge crusts the eyelids shut

associated_symptoms.text: Eyelid crusting or matting, especially on waking

pertinent_negatives: Known contact with someone with viral conjunctivitis

argues_against: Viral upper respiratory infection with conjunctivitis

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not report eye discomfort; parents notice redness, discharge, and matted eyelids, often with irritability.
May present with less prominent redness and discharge, and more non-specific eye discomfort; higher risk of complications if untreated.
Can have more severe, prolonged, or atypical presentation with higher risk of corneal involvement.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, no distress; one or both eyes red with mild discharge
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, keeps dabbing the eye, eyelids matted with discharge
general.severe: Ill-appearing with marked eyelid swelling and copious discharge, photophobia, or eye pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing with severe periocular swelling, proptosis, or systemic signs suggesting orbital or systemic spread

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva and sclera in natural light
findings.finding: Diffuse redness of the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva, most marked peripherally and fading toward the limbus

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lower fornix and lid margins, and ask the patient to blink
findings.finding: Thick yellow-green or mucopurulent discharge pooling in the inferior fornix and crusting the lashes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelid margins and lashes
findings.finding: Crusted or matted eyelashes, often worse on waking

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently palpate the eyelids
findings.finding: Mild diffuse eyelid edema without focal nodule or erythema of the lid skin
Conjunctival edema with a glassy, boggy appearance

findings.maneuver: Evert the lower eyelid and inspect the tarsal conjunctiva
findings.finding: Small lymphoid follicles on the palpebral conjunctiva

findings.maneuver: Evert the upper eyelid and inspect the tarsal conjunctiva
findings.finding: Fine papillae on the tarsal conjunctiva

findings.maneuver: Palpate the preauricular and submandibular lymph nodes
Check visual acuity with a Snellen chart, with correction if worn
findings.finding: Visual acuity at or near the patient's baseline, no decline

findings.maneuver: Shine a light into each eye and observe the direct and consensual response
findings.finding: Brisk, symmetric pupillary constriction with no afferent defect

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea with a penlight, and stain with fluorescein if a corneal lesion is suspected
findings.finding: Clear cornea without opacity, infiltrate, or fluorescein uptake

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to follow a finger through the cardinal directions of gaze
findings.finding: Full, painless eye movements without diplopia

findings.maneuver: Ask about and observe the response to light
findings.finding: No light sensitivity or squinting in bright light

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient whether the eyes itch
Inspect the perilimbal vessels with a penlight
Inspect the eyes from above and below for forward displacement
findings.finding: No proptosis or resistance to retropulsion

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the periorbital skin and lids
findings.finding: No marked periorbital erythema, induration, or tenderness

supporting.why: Identifies the organism and guides therapy when the course is severe, recurrent, or atypical
supporting.only_if: severe, recurrent, or treatment-failure conjunctivitis, or suspected gonococcal or chlamydial infection

supporting.test: Rapid antigen or PCR testing of conjunctival swab for adenovirus
supporting.why: Distinguishes viral from bacterial conjunctivitis when the cause is unclear
supporting.only_if: discharge is watery or the diagnosis is uncertain

not_indicated.why: Bacterial conjunctivitis is a localized infection; the white count is typically normal and does not change management
No role in a superficial eye infection
No role in a superficial eye infection
Not routine for uncomplicated cases; reserved for severe, recurrent, or atypical presentations
not_indicated.only_if: severe, recurrent, or treatment-failure conjunctivitis, or suspected gonococcal or chlamydial infection

not_indicated.test: Rapid antigen or PCR testing of conjunctival swab for adenovirus
not_indicated.why: Not routine; used only when viral conjunctivitis is a strong consideration
not_indicated.only_if: discharge is watery or the diagnosis is uncertain

not_indicated.why: Not needed for conjunctivitis; reserved for suspected orbital cellulitis or abscess
Not routine; performed when a corneal ulcer or keratitis is suspected

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical; do not order routine labs or imaging for typical purulent conjunctivitis
Consider culture and gonococcal/chlamydial testing when there is severe purulent discharge, marked eyelid swelling, or no response to topical antibiotics
Refer urgently if vision is decreased, there is severe pain or photophobia, or the cornea shows fluorescein uptake

differential.name: Viral conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of acute red eye; watery discharge and a viral prodrome can look like a mild bacterial infection

history: Watery rather than purulent discharge
Recent upper respiratory infection or sick contacts
Prominent itching or burning
Often starts in one eye and spreads to the other within days
Highly contagious, often with a known outbreak
exam: Diffuse conjunctival injection with a watery or serous discharge
Follicles on the palpebral conjunctiva, especially the lower lid
Preauricular lymphadenopathy is more common than in bacterial disease
No purulent crusting of the lashes
labs: Adenovirus rapid antigen or PCR positive on conjunctival swab when tested

differential.name: Allergic conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red, irritated eyes with discharge are common in allergy, and patients may describe matting on waking

history: Prominent itching is the hallmark
Bilateral and symmetric involvement
Recurrent seasonal or perennial pattern
Exposure to known allergens such as pollen, dust, or animal dander
No sick contacts
exam: Bilateral conjunctival injection with a stringy or watery discharge
Chemosis and eyelid edema
Cobblestone papillae on the tarsal conjunctiva in chronic cases
Allergic shiners or Dennie-Morgan lines
labs: Eosinophils on conjunctival scraping when performed

differential.name: Bacterial keratitis
differential.why_considered: A red, painful eye with purulent discharge that can be mistaken for conjunctivitis, especially in contact lens wearers
differential.trigger: Contact lens wear with eye pain, photophobia, or decreased vision

history: Contact lens wear, especially overnight or with poor hygiene
Severe eye pain rather than grittiness
Photophobia and tearing
Decreased or blurred vision
exam: Corneal opacity, infiltrate, or fluorescein uptake
Ciliary (perilimbal) injection
Anterior chamber cells or hypopyon in severe cases
Reduced visual acuity
labs: Corneal scraping for culture and Gram stain when a corneal ulcer is present

differential.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: A red, painful eye that can be confused with conjunctivitis if the pain and visual symptoms are not elicited
differential.trigger: Severe eye pain with headache, nausea, or halos around lights

history: Sudden, severe eye or brow pain
Nausea and vomiting
Blurred vision with colored halos around lights
Headache, sometimes mistaken for migraine
exam: Fixed, mid-dilated pupil
Corneal haze or steamy cornea
Markedly elevated intraocular pressure on tonometry
Shallow anterior chamber on penlight exam
Conjunctival injection with a hazy cornea
imaging: Gonioscopy showing a closed angle when performed by an ophthalmologist

differential.name: Orbital cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Eyelid swelling and redness with discharge can be the presenting picture of a deeper orbital infection
differential.trigger: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, or systemic illness

history: Fever and systemic illness
Pain with eye movement
Recent sinusitis or dental infection
Rapidly progressive eyelid swelling
exam: Proptosis and resistance to retropulsion
Painful or restricted extraocular movements
Marked periorbital erythema, induration, and tenderness
Decreased visual acuity or afferent pupillary defect in severe cases
labs: Blood cultures when systemic infection is suspected
imaging: CT orbits with contrast showing orbital fat stranding, abscess, or sinusitis

differential.name: Blepharitis
differential.why_considered: Crusted, matted lashes and red eyes are common in blepharitis and can mimic bacterial conjunctivitis

history: Chronic, recurrent eyelid irritation rather than acute onset
Burning or foreign body sensation along the lid margins
Often bilateral and associated with rosacea or seborrheic dermatitis
exam: Erythema and crusting localized to the eyelid margins
Collarettes or scales around the lash bases
Conjunctival injection is mild and secondary
Meibomian gland dysfunction or chalazia

differential.name: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction
differential.why_considered: Chronic tearing and discharge in infants and adults can resemble infectious conjunctivitis

history: Chronic tearing rather than acute redness
Discharge expressed by pressing over the lacrimal sac
Recurrent episodes in the same eye
Common in infants with a congenital obstruction
exam: Tearing with a normal or minimally injected conjunctiva
Reflux of mucoid or purulent material from the punctum with pressure over the lacrimal sac
Mild redness limited to the medial canthus
imaging: Dacryocystography or CT in atypical or refractory cases

severity.mild: Mild redness and discharge in one eye, no pain, normal vision, no systemic symptoms; often self-limited
severity.moderate: Marked purulent discharge with eyelid crusting and mild discomfort, but vision remains normal and there is no corneal involvement
severity.severe: Copious purulent discharge, marked eyelid swelling, eye pain, or photophobia; may indicate a hyperacute or complicated infection
severity.critical: Not applicable; bacterial conjunctivitis itself is not life-threatening, but gonococcal infection or orbital spread can be sight-threatening or systemic

red_flags.meaning: Suggests corneal involvement, keratitis, or another serious cause of red eye; needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation
Suggests keratitis, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma rather than simple conjunctivitis
Corneal ulcer or keratitis; requires urgent ophthalmology referral

red_flags.finding: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, or marked periorbital swelling
red_flags.meaning: Suggests orbital cellulitis or abscess; needs urgent imaging and IV antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Copious purulent discharge with rapid onset and marked eyelid swelling
red_flags.meaning: Suggests hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis; requires systemic antibiotics and urgent ophthalmology involvement

red_flags.finding: Contact lens wear with pain or vision change
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for bacterial keratitis; remove lens and refer urgently
Consider gonococcal or chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum; requires urgent evaluation and systemic treatment

complications.name: Hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis with corneal perforation
Chronic or recurrent conjunctivitis
clues: Associated blepharitis or nasolacrimal duct obstruction

special_populations.differences: Very common in daycare and school settings; often presents with matted eyelids and irritability rather than reported eye discomfort; usually responds well to topical antibiotics.
Neonatal conjunctivitis can be caused by gonococcus or chlamydia and requires urgent evaluation and systemic treatment; consider nasolacrimal duct obstruction in chronic tearing.
May have less prominent redness and discharge; higher risk of complications and slower healing; consider blepharitis and dry eye as contributing factors.
Higher risk of severe, prolonged, or atypical infection with corneal involvement; lower threshold for culture and ophthalmology referral.
Topical ophthalmic antibiotics are generally considered safe; avoid systemic fluoroquinolones when possible; consider chlamydial infection in the differential.

key_questions.question: When did the redness and discharge start, and how quickly did it come on?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over 1–2 days; a hyperacute course over hours with copious discharge suggests gonococcal infection

key_questions.question: What does the discharge look like — thick and yellow-green, or watery?
key_questions.looking_for: Thick, purulent, yellow-green discharge that crusts the lashes; watery discharge points to viral or allergic causes

key_questions.question: Is it one eye or both, and did it spread from one to the other?
key_questions.looking_for: Often starts in one eye and spreads to the other within a few days; bilateral symmetric itching suggests allergy

key_questions.question: Do your eyes itch?
key_questions.looking_for: Prominent itching argues for allergic conjunctivitis; bacterial disease is gritty or burning rather than itchy

key_questions.question: Is your vision blurry or decreased, and does it clear with blinking?
key_questions.looking_for: Vision should be normal; true vision loss suggests keratitis, uveitis, or glaucoma

key_questions.question: How severe is the pain, and are you bothered by light?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe pain or photophobia suggests corneal involvement or acute angle-closure glaucoma, not simple conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Do you wear contact lenses, and do you sleep in them or clean them properly?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact lens wear with pain or vision change raises concern for bacterial keratitis

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent cold, sore throat, or sick contacts with red eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: A viral prodrome or known outbreak points to viral conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Have you had eye surgery, eye injections, or a foreign body in the eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent ocular surgery or trauma raises the risk of a deeper infection

key_questions.question: Do you have allergies, eczema, or asthma, and is this seasonal?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopy with a seasonal pattern favors allergic conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Are you using any eye drops, ointments, or topical steroids?
key_questions.looking_for: Topical steroids can mask or worsen infection; preserved drops can cause irritation

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or feeling generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic symptoms are unusual and suggest orbital cellulitis or another systemic process

key_questions.question: Is there any chance you could be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Avoid systemic fluoroquinolones in pregnancy; consider chlamydial infection

reasoning_points: Acute onset of redness with thick, purulent, yellow-green discharge that crusts the eyelids, worse on waking
Gritty or burning discomfort rather than prominent itching
Diffuse conjunctival injection that fades toward the limbus, with discharge pooling in the inferior fornix
Visual acuity, pupillary responses, cornea, and extraocular movements are normal
No severe pain, photophobia, proptosis, or periorbital cellulitis
Viral and allergic conjunctivitis considered and made less likely by the purulent discharge and absence of itching or viral prodrome
Serious look-alikes (keratitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, orbital cellulitis) excluded by history and exam
Diagnosis is clinical; routine labs and imaging are not indicated for uncomplicated cases

easy: Child in daycare with one red eye and yellow-green discharge crusting the lashes on waking
Normal vision, no pain, no photophobia
Diffuse conjunctival injection with purulent discharge in the inferior fornix
medium: Adult contact lens wearer with redness and discharge but no pain or vision change
Bilateral involvement with mild eyelid swelling and crusting
Overlap with viral conjunctivitis when discharge is only mildly purulent
Older adult with chronic blepharitis and secondary conjunctival injection
hard: Neonate with purulent eye discharge raising concern for gonococcal or chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum
Hyperacute copious purulent discharge with marked eyelid swelling suggesting gonococcal infection
Contact lens wearer with early keratitis presenting as 'just pink eye'
Patient with recurrent episodes due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction
Immunocompromised patient with prolonged, atypical course and corneal involvement
